analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA power over tobacco, bans most advertising, penalizes makers if teen smoking stays high, and funds health programs from industry payments.
analysis.headline: The Senate debated the bill for a month in 1998, but three votes to cut off debate fell short at 42, 43, and 43 of the 60 needed, and on June 17 a 53-46 vote failed to waive Senate budget rules; the bill went back to committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have turned the 1997 tobacco settlement deal into law. Tobacco companies would have paid billions into a federal trust fund and faced harsh penalties if fewer teenagers did not stop smoking, while the FDA gained authority to regulate cigarette ingredients, advertising, and nicotine levels. In exchange, the companies would have received protection from many future lawsuits, including an annual cap on judgments and an end to addiction and punitive-damage claims. The money would have gone to states for health care costs, anti-smoking programs, help for tobacco farm communities, and veterans' programs.
analysis.who_benefits: State governments reimbursed for treating tobacco-related illness, teenagers who would face far less tobacco advertising and harder-to-get cigarettes, nonsmokers breathing smoke-free public buildings, tobacco farm families receiving transition payments, veterans' programs, and people seeking help to quit smoking.

how_it_helps.text: The FDA would gain authority to regulate tobacco products, including ingredient approval, facility inspections, product performance standards, and authority to require the reduction of nicotine over time.

The bill bans outdoor tobacco advertising, cartoon and human images in ads, colorful point-of-sale advertising, paid product placement in movies and video games, and all tobacco vending machine sales.
Manufacturers would face joint and several financial penalties if underage tobacco use does not fall by required percentages, with additional excise taxes for failing youth-smoking reduction goals.

Participating manufacturers would deposit portions of $10 billion up front plus annual payments into a National Tobacco Settlement Trust Fund that reimburses states for tobacco-related treatment, funds smoking cessation and public education programs, and supports child care.
Tobacco companies would have to open their internal research documents to the public through a National Tobacco Document Depository, with a review board deciding privilege claims.
Tobacco quota holders, farm workers, and tobacco-dependent counties would receive quota loss payments, worker transition assistance, and economic development grants funded by the industry.
The Department of Veterans Affairs would gain the right to recover from tobacco companies the cost of disability compensation attributable to smoking during military service.

analysis.who_pays: Smokers, who would pay higher prices: the bill requires each manufacturer to pass an equal share of its annual settlement payments through to purchasers, and it raises federal excise taxes on tobacco products. Tobacco companies pay the settlement amounts and penalties; retailers face licensing fees and lose vending machine sales.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires manufacturers to pass through to purchasers an equal share of annual settlement payments and raises tobacco excise taxes, so cigarette prices would rise sharply, and since smoking is more common among lower-income people, the cost would fall hardest on them.

In exchange for the payments, participating manufacturers would gain a $6.5 billion annual cap on total judgments, immunity from addiction and dependence claims, termination of state and class-action suits, and protection from punitive damages on settled conduct.
The bill grants participating manufacturers an antitrust exemption allowing them to jointly agree on compliance matters and to refuse to deal with sellers who violate the law.
The bill preempts some stricter state rules on labeling, product standards, and advertising, replacing them with a single federal standard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health gains were large: real penalties tied to falling youth smoking, FDA control over cigarette design and marketing, and tens of billions flowing to state health programs. But the deal was a bargain with the industry, not just a restriction on it: smokers would finance most of it through higher prices, and the companies would trade a known payment schedule for broad protection from the courtroom exposure they then faced, including caps on judgments and an end to addiction-based and punitive-damage claims. Critics on both sides attacked it for exactly this design, and those tradeoffs were central to the fight over the bill.

outcome.mechanism: Republicans refused three times to end debate on the bill, and on the last day it was ruled out of order under Senate budget rules; a 53-46 vote to waive the rule fell short of the 60 needed, and the bill went back to committee, where it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John McCain introduced the bill on November 7, 1997, and it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee.

The Commerce Committee reported the bill with a full substitute amendment on May 1, 1998, and the Finance Committee reported it again with amendments, including new tobacco tax provisions, on May 14, 1998.

The Senate debated the modified substitute from mid-May through mid-June 1998, but three cloture votes to end debate and move to final action failed on June 9, 10, and 11, with only 42, 43, and 43 votes against the 60 needed; not a single Republican voted yes on any of the three.

On June 17, 1998, a fourth cloture vote received 57-42, still short of 60, and a point of order was raised that the bill violated the Congressional Budget Act; the motion to waive the budget rules failed 53-46, the bill was recommitted to the Commerce Committee, and the modified committee substitute fell with it.
The Congress ended January 3, 1999, without the bill ever receiving an up-or-down vote on passage.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers were better off: they avoided the billions in settlement payments, new taxes, advertising bans, and youth-smoking penalties the bill would have imposed, though they also gave up the lawsuit limits it would have granted them. Smokers kept paying the old prices, and states kept pursuing tobacco litigation on their own.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-AZ); chair, Senate Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, managed it through the Commerce Committee, reported the substitute amendment, and presented cloture motions during a month of floor debate.

for.name: Sen. William Roth
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of the Finance Committee with amendments on the ordered deadline, adding the tobacco tax and revenue title.

for.name: 42 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.role: Senate Democrats voting on the first three cloture votes
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on all three early cloture attempts to end debate and advance the bill (42, 43, and 43 of 45 in favor).

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Publicly pressed Congress throughout 1997 and 1998 to enact comprehensive tobacco settlement legislation cutting youth smoking.

against.name: 54 of 55 Senate Republicans
against.role: Senate Republicans voting on the first three cloture votes
against.what_they_did: Voted no on the June 9, 10, and 11 cloture attempts, each of which failed with fewer than the 60 votes needed to end debate.

against.name: Sen. Phil Gramm
against.what_they_did: Made a motion to recommit the bill to the Senate Finance Committee with instructions during floor debate.

against.name: 43 of 55 Senate Republicans
against.role: Senate Republicans voting on the budget-waiver motion
against.what_they_did: Voted no on the June 17 motion to waive the Congressional Budget Act, sustaining the budget point of order against the bill 53-46.

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers
against.role: Major cigarette companies and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Ran an extensive public and advertising campaign in 1997-1998 against comprehensive tobacco settlement legislation and the taxes it would impose.

sides.party_line_note: On the first three votes to end debate, zero of 55 Republicans voted yes while 42 to 43 of 45 Democrats did; on the June 17 budget-waiver vote, 42 of 45 Democrats voted yes against 43 of 55 Republicans voting no.

industries.note: The bill would have required billions in up-front and annual payments, price pass-throughs, excise taxes, strict advertising bans, and penalties if youth smoking did not fall — but in exchange it capped judgments at $6.5 billion a year, barred addiction claims, and gave signatories an antitrust exemption. The industry fought the bill anyway, and its defeat avoided the payments while leaving its courtroom exposure unresolved.

The LEAF Act provisions would have paid farmers for lost quota revenue, funded community development grants in tobacco counties, and provided worker transition and education assistance, all financed by the industry. Growers and warehouse operators also received immunity from actions tied to manufacturers' noncompliance.

industries.industry: Tobacco retailers and vending machine operators
industries.note: Retailers would have faced licensing requirements, a ban on vending machine and self-service sales, and escalating penalties, but vending machine owners would have been reimbursed at fair market value from the trust fund, and compliant retailers could have received compliance bonus grants.

industries.industry: Magazine, billboard, and event sponsorship businesses
industries.note: The bill bans outdoor advertising, cartoon and human imagery, event sponsorships bearing tobacco brand names, and paid product placement in films and video games, eliminating a large slice of tobacco advertising spending. Reduced ad exposure, especially for young people, is the public benefit those outlets would have given up revenue for.
